title: Guru Arjan close
hook: poet, builder, editor and martyr: four names for one life

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Arjan the editor: a weaver, a leatherworker and a Sufi in the same book as the Gurus. Your line was he chose carefully. What did you choose not to pass along? Day one thousand two hundred thirteen.

Four job titles, one life. Poet. Builder. Editor. Martyr. On a résumé they'd look like four different people: one at a desk with a pen, one on a building site with mud on his hands, one sorting pages by lamplight, one standing firm when the powerful came for him. In Sikh memory they're all the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan. We've spent days with his hymns. Today we step back and look at the whole man, and ask what ties the four together.
screen: `POET. BUILDER. EDITOR. MARTYR.` → `FOUR PEOPLE ON A RÉSUMÉ.` → `ONE LIFE: THE FIFTH GURU.`

segments.voice: The poet first. Guru Arjan wrote the Bavan Akhri, the alphabet that ends in grace. He wrote Sukhmani, a name often explained as the jewel of peace, and read for comfort. He wrote tera keeaa meethaa laagai: what You do seems sweet to me. The builder. At Amritsar, around the pool his father began, the Harmandir Sahib rose. Tradition says it was built with doors on every side, open to anyone from any direction. He sang that the Lord Himself stood to finish the saints' work. The editor. Yesterday's book: Gurus and bhagats, chosen carefully, gathered into one volume. And the martyr. History records that he was arrested under the Mughal emperor Jahangir and died in Lahore. Sikh tradition remembers torture, and remembers him meeting it without bitterness; Gurdwara Dera Sahib in Lahore marks the place tradition gives for his death. In the telling, that sweet line comes back: what You do seems sweet to me. So what ties poet, builder, editor and martyr together? Each time, he made a place for other people to stand. A song you can rest inside. A pool and a building you can walk into from any side. A book you can bow to and read. And an example of faith that held under the worst kind of pressure. He didn't build for himself. That's why the line today is poet and builder. Words and walls, both for someone else. On his martyrdom day, Sikhs set up stands by the road and hand cool, sweet water to anyone passing, whoever they are. It's called chhabeel. A sweet drink for a stranger, in memory of a man who called God's will sweet.
screen: `THE POET: ALPHABET, PEACE, SWEETNESS.` · `THE BUILDER: DOORS ON EVERY SIDE.` · `THE MARTYR: LAHORE, WITHOUT BITTERNESS.` · `A PLACE FOR OTHERS TO STAND.` · then, large: `POET AND BUILDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: build or tend one thing. Settle, and breathe. Look around your life for something you've made, or could make, that other people stand in. A family meal. A group chat that's kind. A garden bed. A shelf at work everyone uses. A song you sing to a child. Choose one. Picture what it would need to be a little more open, a little more welcoming, like a door on another side. Hold that picture. Then decide the one small thing you'll do to tend it today. If you pray, you can remember Waheguru on each breath in. The bell holds the time.
Guru Arjan close. Poet, builder, editor and martyr: one life spent making places, in words and in stone, for other people to stand. Today's word.
Your line: poet and builder. Today, do the small thing you found in the sit: one word or one repair that makes a place better for someone else. Day one thousand two hundred thirteen.
